$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 6 & -8\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A$ has the complex eigenvalue $\lambda =-5+3\text{i},$ and that $A=PC{P}^{-1}$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A$ has the complex eigenvalue $\lambda=-2+6\textrm{i},$ and that $A=PCP^{-1}$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, find the matrix $P.$
current_example.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14244484/assets/328c7db70949f7063cc7dc35e0d859228b745d3bcac89271b63bd916b6832e08.svg)

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda.$

Since we are given the eigenvalue $\lambda=-2+6\textrm{i},$ we can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14244484/assets/2508154994907685ad0aea23a520faa1d00c6f9ebfa8368afcee2a25c20d3eb7.svg)

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions to the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =-2+6\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 9 & -5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+6\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3-6\text{i} & -5 \\ 9 & -3-6\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(3-6\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 9{x}_{1}+(-3-6\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
x_1=\dfrac 1 3(1+2\textrm{i})x_2.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14244484/assets/c2b1fe58cfa8594c63030aae534943e1b96a5fb1b144f55764b5f26642af2315.svg)

Setting $x_2=3$, we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14244484/assets/c0da63af3dc7e096501adb8e9c2134caf5c1b39cec3447e99e83c92bc27efa94.svg)

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
